(1) the He I λ10830 line is the best indicator of the primordial abundance, but it is affected by underlying absorption; (2) the He I 2p3s-2p3p transition is the second-best indicator, but it is optically thick and affected by underlying absorption, and (3) the He I lines in H II regions are optically thick and the He/H abundance derived using these lines is not a good indicator of the primodial helium abundance.

In summary, a comprehensive and detailed conclusive statement would be that
there is a 3.5 sigma detection of a primordial He/H abundance of about 0.245, with a 3 sigma error bar of ± 0.015.
the primordial abundance is in the range Yp = 0.240 ± 0.002, with the upper limit of this range being a conservative value, and that there are several reasons to believe that this value is too high.
the primordial helium mass fraction, Yp, is in the range 0.2445 < Yp < 0.2495.
A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
the He/H abundance determination of H II regions is a very difficult task, and that we are still far from having a reliable value for Yp.
the He I lines are too optically thick to be used for the He/H abundance determination.
the He I lines are optically thick, the He I 5876 A line is affected by the underlying absorption lines and the He I 4471 A line by both the underlying absorption and the optical thickness.
The main takeaway from our work is that
there are several sources of error that can affect the Y and O determinations in H II regions, but they are not all independent and, in fact, they can compensate one another.
there is a large uncertainty in Yp due to the He I line intensities, which is the largest source of uncertainty in deriving Yp.
the primordial abundance is likely to be in the range of Yp = 0.2449 ± 0.0020, which is 0.0024 ± 0.0013 higher than the value derived by the Planck Collaboration.
